title: System Design & Distributed Systems Quiz
description: Evaluate your architectural intuition for high-scale distributed systems, consistency models, and fault tolerance.

questions.question: In the CAP Theorem, why can a distributed system with multiple nodes over a physical network never choose 'CA' (Consistency and Availability without Partition Tolerance)?
options: Because hardware load balancers only support round-robin routing.
Because network partitions (dropped packets, severed cables, routing failures) are an inevitable physical reality of distributed networks.
Because the CAP theorem only applies to relational databases like MySQL.
Because ACID transactions cannot be implemented on multi-core processors.
questions.explanation: In distributed systems, network partitions are inevitable. When a partition occurs, nodes cannot communicate. You must either continue serving requests with potentially out-of-date data (favoring Availability - AP) or refuse requests until consistency is restored (favoring Consistency - CP). You cannot avoid partitions.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of the Saga pattern in microservice environments?
options: To speed up SSL/TLS handshakes between microservices.
To coordinate distributed transactions across multiple independent service databases using local transactions and compensating actions.
To automatically compress Kafka event streams.
To enforce OAuth token validation on every microservice boundary.
questions.explanation: Traditional distributed transactions (Two-Phase Commit / 2PC) lock database resources across services and create severe availability bottlenecks. The Saga pattern executes a sequence of local transactions, where each step publishes an event, and failures trigger compensating transactions to rollback business state.

questions.question: How does Consistent Hashing minimize cache reorganization when a server node is added or removed compared to standard modulo hashing (`hash(key) % N`)?
options: It compresses cache keys into 8-bit integers.
It maps both servers and keys onto a circular hash ring, so adding a node only remaps approximately K/N keys (where K is total keys and N is total servers).
It routes all requests to a central in-memory master redis node.
It converts all cache keys into cryptographic public keys.
questions.explanation: In naive modulo hashing, changing N causes almost 100% of keys to remap to new nodes, causing catastrophic cache misses. Consistent hashing maps keys and servers to a 360-degree ring; adding or removing a node only impacts keys between that node and its predecessor (roughly 1/N of total keys).
